When Does Crime Enter House Prices?

When Does Crime Enter House Prices? Evidence from Chicago

Nency Dhameja

Job Market Paper  ·  This version: October 18, 2026

Paper (PDF)Online Appendix
Question

This paper studies which crimes affect house prices, why some do and others do not, and how crime changes whether and how quickly homes sell.

Main finding
I find that most crimes have near-zero effects on housing prices, while a small set lowers them. Of the twenty-two offenses, four carry a sale-price discount across multiple exposure windows (homicide, burglary, narcotics, and vandalism), and two more are statistically significant at a single long-horizon window (disorderly conduct and sex offenses).
All offenses at a glance

Each estimate is the percent change in the sale price per nearby incident (withdrawal: percentage points). The window is how many months of crime before the sale are counted.

The main window, as defined in the paper

Tables that report a single number per offense use the main window of the range over which that offense’s discount is significant at five percent (pooled sample, baseline 0–0.05 versus 0.20–0.30 mile ring), taking the lower of the two main windows when that range has even length, and offenses with no significant window are shown at the median window, six months.

How the comparison works

My identification strategy compares the same property across sales.

Within this comparison, I contrast crime within 0.05 miles of the property, roughly the same block, with crime 0.20 to 0.30 miles away in the same neighborhood.

I estimate this design for all twenty-two offenses and assess it using post-sale crime placebos, which cannot causally affect a price already set.

Figure 1. The near–far design.

Why only some offenses are priced

How buyers use crime information

Price effects are hyperlocal, whereas the predictive content of crime extends beyond the immediate vicinity of the property.

Observability

For the same offense, incidents at a home’s frontage lower prices, while incidents inside the dwelling do not (burglary and narcotics; Table 3).

Relevance

An offense about as frequent near homes as burglary has a discount precisely estimated at zero (motor-vehicle theft).
The transaction

Asking versus closing prices

For the priced offenses, the discount appears at the close rather than in the asking price (Table 4).

Homicide and selling time

A nearby homicide increases time on market: under parcel-by-era fixed effects, the estimate is significant at five percent at seven to nine months, about 15 percent at eight months, or about 2.4 days against a median of 16 in the estimation sample.

Weapons violations and withdrawals

Weapons violations show a particularly consistent withdrawal response. Estimates are positive in all twelve windows under both specifications and statistically significant at the five percent level in eight windows with parcel fixed effects and three with parcel-by-era fixed effects, while the post-off-market placebo is significant in at most one (Table 4; Appendix Table A23).
Rentals

Rents and sale prices

Finally, the offenses that lower asking rents are not always those that lower sale prices.

Which offenses lower rents

Asking-rent reductions appear for offenses with consistent sale-price discounts (burglary) and for offenses with weaker or no detectable sale-price discounts (sex offenses and liquor-law violations), although the rental evidence varies across specifications (Section 5.4).

Narcotics and relisting

Narcotics instead appears in the leasing frictions of Panel B: it raises the probability a listing is a relisting (the unit had an earlier spell on the market) in 11 of 12 windows under each specification, and the result holds across all twenty-two robustness specifications (Figure OF2), with a null future-crime placebo.

How to read these estimates

Near–far estimate \(\delta=(\beta_{\mathrm{near}}-\beta_{\mathrm{far}})\times 100\): percent change per incident within 0–0.05 miles relative to 0.20–0.30 miles (withdrawal: percentage points), pooled 2007–2025, standard errors clustered by tract. PIN: parcel and tract × month fixed effects; PIN×era: parcel-by-era and tract × month fixed effects. Placebo: crime after the transaction. Bars are 95% confidence intervals; drag to zoom, double-click to reset.

One offense, every window

22 offenses × 12 windows × outcomes × 2 specifications × main and placebo; aggregate estimates only.

Robustness

Each check from Section 6 of the paper: the result in one sentence, the tables and figures (links open the PDF), and the estimates.

Reverse Causality and Mean ReversionFigure 3 · Figure A3 · Figure A5 · Table A4

The priced offenses pass this placebo at their main windows and in almost all specifications: post-sale crime is significant in none of the 63 specifications for homicide and vandalism, one for narcotics, and four for burglary (bottom panels of Figure 3 and Appendix Figures A3–A5).

Main vs. post-sale placebo, every window
Predetermined Neighborhood ControlsTable A18

Point estimates change little (Appendix Table A18): a nearby homicide still lowers sale prices by about three percent, and the burglary, narcotics, and vandalism estimates move by hundredths of a percent.

Baseline vs. all five predetermined controls, every window
Cross-Crime ConfoundingTable OA24

Homicide, burglary, and narcotics are nearly uncorrelated with the other offenses in the near ring, and entering all twenty-two offenses’ near–far terms jointly, at a common twelve-month window, leaves each of their discounts nearly identical to its separate estimate (Online Appendix K; Table OA24).

Separate vs. all twenty-two offenses entered jointly, common twelve-month window
Sample SelectionTable OA16 · Table A19

First, I regress the monthly probability of sale on nearby crime for all residential parcels, including those that never sell. Nearby crime does not change this probability: the estimate is statistically indistinguishable from zero (p ≈ 0.4) and small relative to a monthly sale rate of about 0.3 percent.

Third test: hedonic regression on all sales (including homes that sell once) vs. repeat sales, each offense at its main window
Distressed SalesTable OA20

Allowing the near–far effect to differ for distressed sales (REO, short sale, or foreclosure), the discounts are if anything larger among distressed sales, but that subsample is thin near crime and the two differ significantly only for narcotics (Table OA20).

Arms-length vs. distressed sales (REO, short sale, foreclosure), every window
Selection into Zero ExposureFigure OF11 · Figure A1 · Table A2

For burglary the zero-exposure indicator is itself significant (−0.978, s.e. 0.317), so the linear discount is identified partly from the contrast between exposed and unexposed parcels.

Zero-exposure indicator as fixed effects are added, each offense at its main window
Functional FormTable OA23 · Table OA5

Homicide, rare enough that a single incident is effectively the treatment, is significant under every form at its main window (−3.0 to −3.6), whether exposure enters as a raw count, a presence indicator, or in inverse hyperbolic sine.

Raw count vs. presence indicator vs. inverse hyperbolic sine, every window
Spatial Standard ErrorsTable OA21

Conley standard errors at 0.5 and 1.0 km, reported in Table OA21, are close to the clustered ones: homicide (p = 0.016 and 0.029), burglary (p = 0.032 and 0.045), and vandalism (p = 0.020 and 0.045) remain significant at five percent under both cutoffs, and narcotics is significant at five percent at 0.5 km (p = 0.027) and at ten percent at 1.0 km (p = 0.091); inference and the significance stars use the clustered ones.

Priced offenses at their main windows: 95% intervals under each standard error
Specification curves: sale pricesFigure 3 · Figure A3 · Figure A5 · Figure 4 · Figure OF4 · Figure OF7

The discount is significant at five percent in 33 of 63 specifications for vandalism, 29 for narcotics, 29 for burglary, and 15 for homicide, whose point estimates range from about −3.6 percent to about zero with wide intervals.

Show the curves (all 22 offenses; 63 or 103 specifications each)
How to read the curves

Each curve sorts the near–far discount across specifications that vary the exposure window, the fixed effects, the comparison ring, the functional form, and the predetermined controls (Section __SCSEC__). Top: main estimates, sorted; middle: the choices behind each specification; bottom: the post-sale placebo for the same specification. The baseline specification is marked in red.

Spatial Falsification

A falsification test that moves the treatment band outward to 0.05–0.20 leaves narcotics, burglary, and vandalism significant in at most 1 of 48 specifications, indicating effects concentrated within 0.05 miles.

Near ring (0–0.05 mi) vs. outer bands, each against the 0.20–0.30 mi ring, every window
